label: Slow CI reuses one worktree and keeps its build tree between runs
The fast check fits its lanes into 60 s and stops a step at 180 s
Heavy commands take CPU tokens from one pool shared by the whole machine
The Rust tests step takes CPU tokens freed after it starts
Slow-CI runs start at least five minutes apart
The fast Rust lane checks only the crates a change reaches
Rust tests build at opt-level 1
New worktrees keep cargo's view of unchanged files
Full browser sweeps move from slow CI to a run every three hours
The oracle lane plays only scenarios new to the oracles
Beryl 3D's tests, record and gate share one test-profile build, with one integration-test binary per crate
Only beryl_3d and beryl_record link the engine, so an engine edit rebuilds no other Beryl 3D test
The Beryl 3D instruction-count gate counts every frame in one Callgrind run per board, and no bead waits for it before pushing
Every worktree reuses one of ten slot directories, keeping rustc's incremental caches
Clippy builds in its own target directory, and the steps that run beryl_cli share one build before taking CPU tokens
Concurrent ui-test runs keep separate fixture recordings so they do not retry checks after deleting each other's files
Every cargo command, typed or started by `by`, takes CPU tokens and grows its build as tokens come free
Beryl 3D trees clone the cached build directory once, and sweep and coverage trees reuse one path
Lima VMs hold CPU tokens for their cores, run in the background for low-priority work, and stop after 15 idle minutes
Beryl 3D's saved build cache and worktree build directories are held to the 15 GB budget, so each clone copies one build instead of every earlier one
A rebase merges data/beryl3d/gates.json's limits as numbers instead of stopping on a conflict, and a new worktree's Beryl 3D build reuses the cached build instead of rebuilding every crate
The fast check's Beryl 3D steps run in four lanes at once, with clippy in its own target and builds waiting without tokens
Beryl 3D's export command writes the recordings on as many threads as its CPU tokens allow

Every six hours each worktree's rust/target and rust/beryl3d/target delete the builds that newer builds of the same units replaced, deleting them in the background, so a reused slot holds one build instead of a day's worth
Agents send their file reads and searches in one message instead of one request per read, and beads name files by path so a session can read them all at once
Beryl 3D timeline parity reuses the shared build for export and timeline playback
Sweep step replays skip the sweep's lock, and waited-for runs go first on the bench VM
The fast check's Beryl 3D interface tests run the b3d of the shared build instead of building b3d alone, so the cargo-test and timeline-parity lanes no longer wait behind that build
Each fast-check lane reads per-hour and per-day sums of the run log instead of scanning the whole 1.4 GB file twice, so choosing and timing its checks takes under half a second

An agent's cargo build gives its spare CPU tokens back while a push waits, and a push that would start short waits up to 10 s for them, so a push's fast-check steps stop running on one core beside long agent builds

A flaky check files its delete bead only when it flakes again in another run within a week, so one-off problems of a run (load, a shared fixture, code changing between attempts) no longer start an Opus session each
A Beryl 3D program in a fast check (record, b3d test) takes more CPU tokens while it runs as other steps release them, and adds threads, instead of keeping the one to three tokens it started with
Beryl 3D reuses placement lookups while compiling scripts and visits fewer effects for each card
Beryl 3D's fast-check cargo-test runs only the tests that fit the time left
Single-threaded b3d commands take one CPU token instead of twelve
An agent's cargo build starts at once on the CPU tokens that are free and grows as slow CI and the sweeps give theirs back, instead of waiting up to 10 s for them

The commands `just b3d tree`, `png` and `film` start their rebuild without waiting for CPU tokens, run their one-thread program outside the pool, and build `dev` without ThinLTO, so a one-line edit to `beryl_scene` shows in about 3 s instead of 4 to 127 s

The fast check's Beryl 3D cargo-test step runs its tests in waves when its CPU lease got fewer tokens than it wanted, taking the tokens that free up before each wave, instead of running every test on the 1-2 threads it started with (60-115 s on one thread against 18-25 s on twelve)

Push and queue cargo builds, and growing programs such as Beryl 3D's record, start at once on the CPU tokens that are free and hold lower classes back while they grow, instead of waiting up to 10 s for elastic tokens before a build or record that usually has nothing to do
Beryl 3D's fast-check test steps stop at the run's target, after at least 45 s of tests, instead of filling the time up to the 180 s hard limit
Card writers can omit hand-written scenarios when generated scenarios cover every mutant and pass the oracle check

A push's fast check runs in one of three reused check trees, check-1 to check-3, which stay a commit or two behind staging and keep their rustc incremental caches, instead of in the pushing tree, which rebuilt every crate staging changed since its agent started (Beryl 3D shared test build: median 134 CPU-seconds per push)
Card writers start from a Rust draft and see vocabulary and example files only for unresolved clauses

The fast check's pytest step runs the Python test files that fit its window, those the change edits or whose imports reach it first, and stops at the window's end, instead of all 855 tests on any tools/ change (median 93 s, cut off at 180 s in a quarter of runs), and the browser sweep runs the whole suite

A flaky-check bead and its repeat comments quote the failed attempt's output, kept for 14 days in $BERYL_CACHE/ci/flakes, instead of naming only the step and sending an Opus session to look for logs that the rerun and the Beryl 3D sweep had already overwritten (6 such beads for whole steps open on 2026-11-17)

The `just b3d timeline-parity` command names Beryl 3D's timeline file by nanosecond and process id, and writes the web timeline cache by rename, so the Beryl 3D sweep's timeline-parity and timeline-parity-all steps, which run at once and share $BERYL_CACHE/b3d, no longer delete or half-read each other's files (the cause behind flaky-check beads by-o3wua and by-s9etj)

A nightly-failure bead quotes its own step's output and names a file that keeps it for two weeks, instead of the tail of the whole night (which ended with the oracle and iroh steps) in a file the next firing overwrote, so a Steward no longer re-runs a 2-10 minute `just fuzz` just to see what failed
Enact replaces local sync and its 4.7 s median ownership-lock wait with tk coordination
Enact tk documents every option, provides offline agent guidance and supports --brief discovery output so sessions avoid loading full ticket bodies to select work
Beryl 3D's record command runs the linker's executable so warm builds reuse its macOS first-run validation instead of launching Cargo's refreshed copy
Oracle outcomes use each scenario’s exported inputs so unrelated exporter edits retain prior passes
Native builds avoid stale LLVM-symbol links and manual cleans by disabling incremental reuse only for dependencies, while native workspace edits remain incremental

Python tests that run a fake ui-test, shots, script or oracle lane no longer start the real workspace cargo build from inside pytest, where four tests spent 37-59 s each in it, about 190 test-seconds and 500 CPU-seconds per full run in a fresh worktree

Beryl 3D's parity-list check runs in the fast check's repo lane on every change instead of only in the 3-hourly Beryl 3D sweep, so a deleted or added skill fails at push time rather than leaving the sweep red, re-bisected and re-commented every run until a session takes the ticket

The switch from Enact to Ignite: Ignite builds, checks and lands every change and holds the tickets, with checks chosen by input hashes, a shared result cache and scores in place of Enact's fast check, slow CI, sweeps, nightly, CPU token pool and role files
Tip verification lists each family once per round, runs families in parallel landing trees, builds the whole workspace when a subset's features differ, and leaves a waiting tip for ten minutes
Kept listings (memory, local, hub) and the landing gate deciding which families a change can affect before it lists or builds anything
Tip claims sized by measured cost instead of 50 checks, and a covered family (b3d-interface) not run beside the family that covers it
Two budgets: the gate runs 60 s of checks at the landing rate on what its tree has already built, leaving checks that need a cold build to tip verification
Two budgets: master moves after 300 s of the best-scored tip checks, the rest running after it moves
`just b3d cargo-test -p` filters the shared workspace build instead of building the named crates again: 74 crates and 689 CPU-s (310 s wall) after the shared build, now 0 crates and 1 CPU-s
Compiling grants give cores back to waiters of their own class past a fair share: 15 agent requests had queued 148-164 s behind one 12-core build
Tree sweep keeps every unit a kept build reaches (it deleted 35 live build-script runs of 23 crates in one tree), and compiling tickets prefer a tree holding the build directory beside their files

Quick commands (last 5+ runs each under 2 CPU-s, not Cargo) start without waiting for a core: `uv sync` for the Python environment used at most 1.2 CPU-s but queued up to 726 s before listing any family
Grants whose commands leave cores idle lend them to waiting requests: every core was granted for an hour while the machine stayed half idle and requests queued
Landings that change only Ignite run its fmt, clippy and tests on reserved cores in a fixed warm tree instead of the gate: four Ignite fixes waited 10 to 30 minutes in the scheduler they were fixing

A landing that loses the race for the tip keeps its landing tree and re-gates only the families the commits landed since touch: before, each lost race re-ran the whole gate, often in another tree that built again (2-pass landings took 28 minutes against 7 for one pass)
The Rust adapter imports the card modules only for the card-text family, and `allocations` lists without a build: a comment edited in card.py made a landing wait 40 minutes on a cold rust-tests build

The daemon's launchd agent is Interactive: under Standard every Ignite command ran at utility priority on the slower cores, doing half the work per CPU-second while load reached 53 with 56% of the CPU idle

A compiling lease starts from an APFS copy of the build of the tree nearest the tip: in a second tree the cli, test-binary and release fuzz-test builds took 5.4, 6.3 and 0.2 CPU-s, against cold medians of 947, 1,070 and 1,390 CPU-s

A change confined to the express paths judges a family with no kept listing by its declared inputs: a change touching only Ignite's files selected 637 checks, built `b3d` (310 CPU-s) and gated twice, about 95 s each

Ignite's own tests run under cargo-nextest, from the test build, and fmt and clippy no longer wait for that build: warm on 2026-11-18 at load 30 to 43 the 1325 tests took 13.2 s wall and 59 CPU-s against 35 s and 91 CPU-s through `cargo test`, which ran the 29 test binaries one after another; clippy re-checked the workspace in about 4 s

The monitor rewrites a daemon launchd agent an older build wrote: hours after the agent became Interactive, jarvis still ran every rustc at utility priority, ten of them at a quarter core each with 40% of the CPU idle, because only `ignite install` wrote the agent

`ignite test` of Ignite's own checks, and `ignite check`, run the express commands on the reserved express cores when the tree changes only Ignite: through the scheduler they took 5 to 8.5 minutes while other builds held its cores, against 40 s warm on 3 express cores after a daemon edit (fmt 0 s, clippy 2 s, nextest 38 s)

The Claude dispatcher's settings deny the tools its loop never calls, which Claude Code then leaves out of its context: the desktop app's browser, simulator, chart, terminal and editing tools took about 60,000 of its 120,000-token window before its first message, so each request re-sent them and it compacted after about 27,000 tokens of loop

Ignite's release build is incremental and its dev and test profiles keep only line tables: after a daemon-only edit the release rebuild took 75 s on 3 cores and now takes about 4 s, and the express commands (clippy, test build and nextest run) took 85 s and now take about 70 s
